lessons.title: The WHO 2021 semen analysis: what to order, how to collect it and how to read it
lessons.objective: Interpret the semen analysis with the WHO 2021 lower reference limits without treating them as a fertility threshold, recognise collection errors, and know when to repeat it.
lessons.closing: The semen analysis is necessary but not conclusive: weigh collection, repeat testing and the set of parameters before labelling a man.

lessons.title: Clinical evaluation of the man: hormones, genetics, varicocele and what not to order
lessons.objective: Decide the next step after a confirmed abnormal semen analysis, apply the AUA/ASRM and NICE genetic thresholds, and recognise tests and treatments that are not recommended.
lessons.closing: The male evaluation is targeted: examination and hormones first; genetics, imaging and DNA fragmentation only with a specific indication; no exogenous testosterone.

lessons.title: Antioxidants and supplements in men: what the evidence says
lessons.objective: Explain the AUA/ASRM, NICE and ESHRE positions on male supplements, read the 2022 Cochrane review without over-interpreting it, and counsel the couple.
lessons.closing: Semen parameters, pregnancy and live birth are different outcomes: today no guideline supports a specific antioxidant, and the advice centres on habits and not delaying the work-up.

items.title: The man is assessed from the start, not “if her tests are normal”
items.core: AUA/ASRM recommends starting concurrent assessment of both partners (expert opinion), including a reproductive history in the initial evaluation of the man (clinical principle) and, in addition, one or more semen analyses (strong recommendation; evidence level B). NICE offers both partners assessment after 1 year of unprotected intercourse when there is no known or suspected cause (1.16.5). [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
AUA/ASRM estimates that a male factor is solely responsible in about 20% of infertile couples and contributory in another 30–40%, while acknowledging that the true prevalence is not well defined because of differing definitions and populations. Without an adequate male evaluation, the female partner may end up with unnecessary, costly or invasive treatment. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

The semen analysis informs on testicular production (reflected in total sperm number), patency and function of the genital tract, secretions of the accessory glands, and emission and ejaculation. When the cause of an abnormal semen analysis is not identified, the guideline calls it idiopathic male infertility (about 30% of men with an abnormal semen analysis). [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

Home or mail-in semen test kits are no substitute for analysis in a specialised andrology laboratory: the guideline warns that their accuracy varies and that results cannot be extrapolated from one test to another. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.recall: At minimum, what should the initial evaluation of the man include according to AUA/ASRM, and when is it done relative to the woman?
items.pearl: Order the semen analysis at the same visit as her tests: it is not the last step of the work-up.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: AUA/ASRM 2020 (amended 2024): strong, grade B for the semen analysis only; clinical principle for the reproductive history and expert opinion for concurrent assessment. NICE 2026.

items.title: WHO 2021 values: lower reference limits (5th centile)
items.core: The WHO manual, 6th edition (2021), publishes the 5th centile of results from about 3500 men in 12 countries whose partners achieved a natural conception with time to pregnancy ≤12 months: volume 1.4 ml; concentration 16 × 10⁶/ml; total number 39 × 10⁶/ejaculate; total motility 42%; progressive 30%; vitality 54%; normal forms 4%. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]
items.body:
Table 8.3 (5th centile; 95% CI): volume 1.4 ml (1.3–1.5); concentration 16 × 10⁶/ml (15–18); total number 39 × 10⁶/ejaculate (35–40); total motility 42% (40–43); progressive 30% (29–31); vitality 54% (50–56); normal forms 4% (3.9–4.0). The reference population had 2–7 days of abstinence and excluded men attending infertility clinics. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]

The manual states that the lower fifth percentile does not represent a limit between fertile and infertile men, that there is substantial overlap between the two groups, that fertility should be understood as a continuum, and that the manual is not a guideline for clinical decisions. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]

Guidelines do use them as a practical reference: NICE asks you to compare the first semen analysis with these values (adding a pH of 7.2 or more) and notes they are valid only for the techniques described by WHO (1.17.1); ESHRE considers a result below the 5th percentile and its confidence interval clinically relevant for deciding on further investigation. AUA/ASRM refers to lower reference limits (LRL) based on the lower 5th centile of fertile men; its text cites the 6th edition, but its table and figures still use 5th-edition (2010) values, for example <15 million/ml for oligozoospermia. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.recall: Which population does the WHO 2021 5th centile come from, and what does it NOT represent?
items.pearl: Teach each figure with its full name: “5th centile of men whose partner conceived within ≤12 months”, not “minimum to be fertile”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: WHO laboratory manual (not a clinical guideline); its use as a clinical reference is endorsed by NICE 2026, ESHRE 2023 and AUA/ASRM.

items.title: Myth: “It is in range, so there is no male factor” (and the reverse)
items.core: A value above or below the lower limit does not by itself predict fertility or infertility: the semen analysis cannot precisely distinguish fertile from infertile men except in azoospermia and some extreme pictures (complete globozoospermia, necrozoospermia, complete asthenozoospermia), and it carries more weight when several abnormalities coincide. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.body:
AUA/ASRM describes semen parameters as highly variable biological measures, advises considering them collectively rather than individually, and notes that the more parameters fall below the lower limit the greater the probability of subfertility risk, without being predictive for the individual. Some men with abnormal parameters have achieved natural conceptions. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

WHO adds that some couples conceive within a year despite ejaculate problems, and that other men with a normal ejaculate are classed as infertile mainly because of female factors. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]

A “normal” semen analysis can also hide sperm that do not function well: AUA/ASRM states that after failed assisted reproduction cycles or with recurrent pregnancy loss the man should be evaluated, considering karyotype and sperm DNA fragmentation testing. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

Be cautious with morphology: WHO notes its limited prognostic value for spontaneous pregnancy and ART outcome, and that statistically distinguishing 3% from 5% normal forms in an individual requires assessing 1500 spermatozoa by highly trained staff. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]
items.recall: Why does an in-range semen analysis not exclude a male factor, and a slightly out-of-range one not confirm it?
items.application: Faced with one isolated value slightly below the limit, look at the whole picture, repeat, and put it in context before giving a verdict.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: AUA/ASRM (expert opinion and guideline text); WHO manual 2021.

items.title: Before interpreting: how the sample is collected
items.core: WHO asks for a complete ejaculate collected after a minimum of 2 and a maximum of 7 days of abstinence and analysed ideally within 30 minutes (60 at most); losing the first, sperm-rich fraction alters the result more than losing the last one. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]
items.body:
Collection: the sample must be complete and the man must report any loss; collection in a private room close to the laboratory is recommended; ordinary latex condoms must not be used (they contain agents that interfere with motility) and lubricants are avoided unless validated as non-spermatotoxic. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]

Abstinence: WHO acknowledges that the 2–7-day interval is based on clinical experience and may contribute to variability and to a blurred limit between normal and subfertile results; its influence is hard to quantify. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]

ASRM (2022) notes that abstinence intervals longer than 5 days may adversely affect sperm counts and that 2 days is already associated with normal densities; in a retrospective study of almost 10,000 specimens, in men with normal semen quality concentration and motility remained normal even with daily ejaculation, and at 10 days or more parameters begin to deteriorate. [[ref:asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility]]
items.recall: What abstinence interval does WHO recommend, what is it based on, and which ejaculate fraction matters most not to lose?
items.application: Before repeating “just in case”, ask about abstinence, lost fractions, the container used, and time to the laboratory.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: WHO itself bases the 2–7 days on clinical experience; the ASRM data on abstinence are observational and retrospective.

items.title: What I would do with a semen analysis below the limit
items.core: According to the expert position cited by ESHRE, a single high-quality ejaculate is enough to decide the next steps, and if there are abnormalities it is repeated: ESHRE after a 3-month interval, NICE ideally at 3 months (sooner if there is azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia), and AUA/ASRM advises considering at least two analyses a month apart. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.body:
ESHRE recommends at least one basic WHO semen analysis in a laboratory with external quality control and, if the result is below the 5th-percentile reference limit (6th edition), repeating it after a 3-month interval. NICE offers a confirmatory repeat test (1.17.3) ideally at 3 months, to allow the cycle of spermatozoa formation to be completed, and as soon as possible if a gross deficiency (azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia) has been detected (1.17.4). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

AUA/ASRM does not set 3 months: it states that, because of biological variability, at least two semen analyses a month apart should be considered, especially if the first is abnormal. This difference in interval is real; what the three sources share is not deciding on a single abnormal result. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

With 2 or more abnormal semen analyses, NICE offers physical examination of the scrotum and testes and suggests considering serum testosterone and gonadotrophins (1.17.5); AUA/ASRM asks male reproductive experts to evaluate men with abnormal parameters or presumed male infertility with a complete history and examination. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.recall: After how many months is an abnormal semen analysis repeated according to ESHRE and NICE, and what does AUA/ASRM propose?

rows.text: Semen analysis 1: complete sample, 2–7 days of abstinence, quality-controlled laboratory
Within the limit: one high-quality ejaculate is enough to decide (ESHRE)
Below the limit: repeat (ESHRE/NICE ideally at 3 months; AUA at least two analyses a month apart)
Azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia: repeat as soon as possible (NICE)

visual.alt: Flow diagram: well-collected initial semen analysis; if within the limit one high-quality ejaculate is enough; if below, repeat (at 3 months per ESHRE and NICE, sooner for azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia; AUA at least two analyses a month apart); with two or more abnormal, physical examination and consider testosterone and gonadotrophins.

items.application: Record the date, abstinence and any collection problems on the report: without them you cannot compare two semen analyses.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023 and NICE 2026 agree on the 3-month interval; AUA/ASRM proposes one month (guideline text). Certainty not graded for the interval.

items.stem: Carla (33, fictional) and Diego (36) have not conceived after 15 months. Diego’s first semen analysis, with a complete sample, 4 days of abstinence and a quality-controlled laboratory, shows a concentration of 10 × 10⁶/ml and a total number of 20 × 10⁶ per ejaculate: both below the WHO 5th centile. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Diagnose male infertility and refer directly to ICSI.
options.why: A single result below the 5th centile is not a diagnosis: WHO itself states it is not a limit between fertile and infertile men, and ESHRE and NICE ask for a repeat.

options.text: Repeat the semen analysis (ideally at 3 months) and interpret it together with the history and examination.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE (below the WHO 5th centile) advises repeating it after a 3-month interval and NICE (abnormal result) ideally at 3 months; AUA/ASRM, at least two analyses a month apart.

options.text: Do nothing: the 5th centile is not a fertility limit, so the result is irrelevant.
options.why: Not being a fertility limit does not make it irrelevant: ESHRE considers a result below the 5th centile and its confidence interval clinically relevant for deciding on further investigation.

options.text: Order sperm DNA fragmentation immediately to decide the assisted reproduction technique.
options.why: NICE advises against this test and AUA/ASRM does not recommend it in the initial evaluation of the infertile couple.

items.explanation: The first step with a low semen analysis is to confirm it under adequate conditions and put it in context; the WHO figures are lower reference limits, not a verdict.

items.stem: In another semen analysis, Diego (4 days of abstinence) says he lost “the first spurt” while collecting the sample. The report shows a concentration of 12 × 10⁶/ml. How should you interpret it?

options.text: It is reliable: concentration does not depend on which fraction of the ejaculate is lost.
options.why: The first fractions are sperm-rich (prostatic fluid) and later ones are dominated by seminal vesicle fluid, so losing the first one does change the concentration.

options.text: It is reliable: what matters most is losing the last fraction, not the first.
options.why: It is the other way round: per WHO, losing the first, sperm-rich portion has more influence than losing the last.

options.text: The sample is incomplete: do not treat it as definitive and repeat it collecting the whole ejaculate after 2–7 days of abstinence.
options.why: Correct: WHO requires a complete ejaculate and any loss of a fraction must be reported; the repeat should use proper collection and 2–7 days of abstinence.

options.text: Repeat it after 14 days of abstinence to compensate for the lost fraction.
options.why: A long abstinence does not compensate for incomplete collection: WHO sets a maximum of 7 days and ASRM notes that parameters begin to deteriorate at 10 days or more.

items.explanation: The reliability of a semen analysis starts with collection: an incomplete sample or one outside the abstinence interval cannot be used to classify a man.

items.stem: Diego’s semen analysis is normal by WHO criteria (no other clinical abnormalities). Diego asks for anti-sperm antibodies “to be sure”. What do you answer?

options.text: They are not ordered routinely: NICE advises against offering them, ESHRE does not recommend them with a normal semen analysis and AUA/ASRM does not perform them in the initial evaluation.
options.why: Correct: the three sources agree on not ordering them in the initial evaluation (NICE 1.17.2; ESHRE, strong with very low certainty; AUA/ASRM, expert opinion).

options.text: Order them, because if positive systemic corticosteroids are given and fertility improves.
options.why: NICE states that the significance of anti-sperm antibodies and the effectiveness of systemic corticosteroids should be explained as uncertain (1.24.4).

options.text: Order anti-sperm antibodies in Carla’s serum, which are recommended.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend serum anti-sperm antibodies for either partner in unexplained infertility either (strong).

options.text: Repeat the semen analysis at 3 months, because ESHRE always requires it.
options.why: ESHRE asks for a 3-month repeat when the first one is below the WHO 5th centile, not when it is normal.

items.explanation: With a normal semen analysis, no treatment decision depends on anti-sperm antibodies: ordering them adds cost and anxiety without changing the plan.

items.title: What I would do: history, examination and hormones when the semen analysis is abnormal
items.core: With 2 or more abnormal semen analyses, NICE offers examination of the scrotum and testes and suggests considering serum testosterone and gonadotrophins (1.17.5). AUA/ASRM asks for FSH and testosterone when there is impaired libido, erectile dysfunction, oligozoospermia or azoospermia, atrophic testes, or evidence of a hormonal abnormality on examination (expert opinion). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.body:
The NICE committee considers examination of the scrotum and testes an essential part of the assessment: it can detect underlying causes such as varicocele and testicular cancer, and it is simple and low cost. NICE also recommends asking about drugs and other products that can affect fertility (for example testosterone-replacement therapy, finasteride, anabolic steroids or cannabis) (1.13.1). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

AUA/ASRM reminds that male infertility can occasionally be the presenting manifestation of a serious underlying condition (such as a testicular or pituitary tumour) and that 1% to 6% of men evaluated for infertility have significant undiagnosed disease, including malignancy, even with a “normal” semen analysis. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

On blood tests, AUA/ASRM does not consider endocrine evaluation a first-line test for every man: it is indicated when clinical findings or sexual function suggest an endocrinopathy, and suggested in oligozoospermia, particularly with a concentration <10 million/ml. Testosterone is drawn in the morning (8–10 a.m.); if fasting total testosterone is low (<300 ng/dL), it is repeated together with free or bioavailable testosterone, LH, estradiol and prolactin. A “normal” FSH does not guarantee intact spermatogenesis. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

In unexplained infertility with a normal semen analysis, ESHRE does not recommend serum hormonal testing (strong). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: What do you do after 2 abnormal semen analyses according to NICE, and when is the testosterone sample drawn according to AUA/ASRM?
items.application: Record everything the man takes (including “boosters” and gym products) in the history before ordering hormones.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: NICE 2026 (1.17.5, 1.13.1); AUA/ASRM: expert opinion for hormonal evaluation; ESHRE 2023: strong against with a normal semen analysis (very low certainty).

items.title: What I would not order up front: scrotal ultrasound, TRUS/MRI and biopsy
items.core: AUA/ASRM advises against routine scrotal ultrasound in the initial evaluation, transrectal ultrasound or pelvic MRI, and diagnostic testicular biopsy to distinguish obstructive from non-obstructive azoospermia (expert opinion). ESHRE also does not recommend testicular imaging with a normal semen analysis (strong). [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
Scrotum: ultrasound is not recommended routinely to investigate a presumed varicocele, because treating non-palpable ones is not associated with improved semen parameters or fertility rates. It can be used if examination is difficult (for example obesity or a highly contracted dartos), to confirm a varicocele before repair, or to assess treatment success by shared decision-making. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

TRUS or pelvic MRI: AUA/ASRM reserves them for men whose semen analysis suggests ejaculatory duct obstruction (acidic, azoospermic semen with volume <1.4 ml, normal serum testosterone and palpable vas deferens). Renal ultrasound is recommended in vasal agenesis. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

Isolated right varicocele: routine abdominal imaging is not recommended if it is small or moderate; a retrospective study of more than 4000 men with varicocele found no difference in cancer diagnoses by laterality, although the guideline does recommend considering abdominal imaging for a new-onset or non-reducible varicocele, especially if large. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.recall: In which situation does AUA/ASRM contemplate TRUS or pelvic MRI, and what does it ask for in vasal agenesis?
items.pearl: An imaging test is ordered for a specific clinical question, not to “complete” the work-up.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: AUA/ASRM: expert opinions (“not routinely”); ESHRE 2023: strong against testicular imaging with a normal semen analysis (very low certainty).

items.title: Male genetics: when to order karyotype, Y microdeletion and CFTR
items.core: AUA/ASRM and NICE agree on offering karyotype, Y microdeletion and CFTR testing only in specific pictures (azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia, and obstruction or absence of the vas), but their thresholds differ: AUA/ASRM uses a concentration ≤1 × 10⁶/ml for Y microdeletion and <5 × 10⁶/ml for karyotype, accompanied by elevated FSH, testicular atrophy or impaired sperm production; NICE uses <1 × 10⁶/ml (idiopathic) and “consider” karyotype if persistently <5 × 10⁶/ml. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
AUA/ASRM: karyotype in men with primary infertility and azoospermia or concentration <5 million/ml accompanied by elevated FSH, testicular atrophy or a diagnosis of impaired sperm production (expert opinion); Y-chromosome microdeletion in azoospermia or concentration ≤1 million/ml with those same conditions (moderate recommendation; grade B); CFTR (including the 5T allele) in vasal agenesis or idiopathic obstructive azoospermia, and genetic evaluation of the partner if the man carries a CFTR mutation or has no vas deferens (expert opinion). The text adds that an abnormal karyotype is present in about 6% of all infertile men. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

NICE 2026: Y microdeletion in idiopathic azoospermia or concentration <1 million/ml (1.17.7); CFTR in idiopathic suspected obstructive azoospermia or a vasal abnormality (1.17.8); karyotype in idiopathic azoospermia and consider it if persistent concentration is <5 million/ml (1.17.9–1.17.10); genetic counselling when there is a specific genetic defect (1.17.11). With an AZFa or AZFb microdeletion, NICE advises against offering surgical sperm retrieval (1.26.1), because its success is very low; the committee notes that an AZFc microdeletion does not affect retrieval success. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

The 1 million/ml threshold in NICE is a committee consensus, based on the vast majority of microdeletions occurring at concentrations ≤1 million/ml. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What is the difference between AUA/ASRM and NICE in the concentration threshold for Y microdeletion testing?
items.application: Before ordering genetics, check the concentration, whether it is persistent, and whether FSH is elevated or there is atrophy: the indication depends on the guideline you follow.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: AUA/ASRM: expert opinion except Y microdeletion (moderate, B); NICE 2026: the 1 million/ml threshold for Y microdeletion was set by committee consensus.

items.title: Varicocele: when repair is considered and what evidence supports it
items.core: AUA/ASRM advises considering varicocelectomy in men attempting to conceive with a palpable varicocele, infertility and abnormal semen parameters, except in azoospermia (moderate recommendation; grade B), and not recommending it for non-palpable varicoceles detected only by imaging (strong; grade C). NICE suggests considering radiological or surgical treatment if the varicocele is detected on examination, they are trying to conceive spontaneously and semen parameters are reduced, taking female factors into account (1.28.1). [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
Frequency: varicoceles occur in about 15% of adult men and 40% of infertile men; 85% are left-sided and unilateral. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

What we know about the result: in the Wang et al. meta-analysis cited by AUA/ASRM, assuming a 17% pregnancy rate without treatment, the estimated rate with subinguinal microsurgical varicocelectomy was 42% (95% CI 26–61%); the guideline itself warns this must be interpreted with caution because it includes non-randomised studies and selective outcome reporting. NICE found higher pregnancy rates with treatment in the subgroup with clinical varicocele and abnormal semen analysis, but very few studies reported live birth and those that did gave mixed results. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Before assisted reproduction: a meta-analysis of 7 retrospective non-randomised studies (clinical varicocele) estimated pregnancy and live birth odds 1.76-fold higher after repairing the varicocele before ART (AUA/ASRM), whereas NICE identified no RCTs on treating varicocele before assisted conception and therefore makes no recommendation for that population. In men with varicocele and non-obstructive azoospermia, AUA/ASRM asks to inform that there is no definitive evidence supporting repair before sperm retrieval. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Which three conditions define the indication to repair a varicocele, and which varicocele should NOT be repaired?
items.pearl: Palpable + infertility + abnormal parameters (without azoospermia), trying to conceive spontaneously and taking female factors into account: that is when repair is considered; a varicocele seen only on ultrasound is not repaired.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: Moderate recommendation (AUA/ASRM, grade B) and “consider” (NICE); the pregnancy benefit comes largely from non-randomised studies and live-birth data are scarce.

items.title: Do not prescribe exogenous testosterone to a man seeking fertility
items.core: AUA/ASRM states that exogenous testosterone should not be prescribed to men interested in current or future fertility (clinical principle), and NICE advises against offering androgens to treat semen abnormalities (1.24.3). [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
Mechanism and reversibility: long-acting testosterone exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary and can inhibit gonadotrophin secretion; depending on the degree of suppression, spermatogenesis decreases or ceases (oligo- or azoospermia). Recovery of sperm in the ejaculate occurs in most azoospermic men after stopping it, but may take months or, rarely, years, and some men never fully recover their sperm production. With a short-acting nasal testosterone, spermatogenesis was preserved in two studies, but long-term data are lacking and the guideline does not advise it routinely. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

NICE found no evidence of improved pregnancy rates with androgens and comments that they may even harm fertility. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

When there is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, NICE offers gonadotrophins (1.24.1) and AUA/ASRM asks to investigate the aetiology and treat according to the diagnosis. In other cases the guidelines differ: NICE reserves gonadotrophins or anti-oestrogens for clinical trials (1.24.2), whereas AUA/ASRM allows considering aromatase inhibitors, hCG or SERMs in men with low testosterone (conditional; grade C) and an FSH analogue in idiopathic infertility (conditional; grade B), and notes that, in idiopathic infertility, SERMs have limited benefits relative to ART results (expert opinion). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]
items.recall: Why can exogenous testosterone leave a man azoospermic, and how long can recovery take?
items.application: If the man is already using testosterone, the first step of the fertility consultation is to discuss it with the team that prescribed it.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: AUA/ASRM: clinical principle; NICE 2026 (1.24.3): do not offer androgens. Treatments for other hormonal scenarios: conditional (AUA/ASRM) or trial-only (NICE).

items.title: Sperm DNA fragmentation: what each guideline says
items.core: NICE advises against the test (1.17.6); AUA/ASRM does not recommend it in the initial evaluation of the infertile couple (moderate; grade C) but does recommend it in recurrent pregnancy loss (moderate; grade C); ESHRE does not recommend it with a normal semen analysis in unexplained infertility (strong), the ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guideline says it could be considered for diagnostic purposes (conditional), and the add-ons document finds insufficient evidence to use it to predict pregnancy or guide treatment. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
Why: NICE reasons that there is no effective treatment, that the assays are expensive and take weeks, that the link between elevated fragmentation and subfertility has not been established, and that it is unclear which test and threshold to use. ESHRE notes that assays are not interchangeable, their thresholds are not standardised, and no study has tested whether performing the test changes the couple’s outcomes. AUA/ASRM agrees on the lack of prospective studies on its impact on management and on inconsistent cut-offs. WHO describes it as a technique and as a promising biomarker only partially related to semen quality. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]

Where AUA/ASRM recommends it: with recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more), evaluate the man with karyotype (expert opinion) and DNA fragmentation (moderate recommendation; grade C); and it may be useful after repeated IVF failures. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] ESHRE (recurrent pregnancy loss, 2022) is more cautious: fragmentation “could be considered” for diagnostic purposes using a validated test (conditional), and parental karyotyping is not routine but follows an individual risk assessment (conditional). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

What to do with an elevated result: this is the point of greatest disagreement. AUA/ASRM states that testicular sperm may be considered in non-azoospermic men with an elevated fragmentation index (clinical principle), but acknowledges that data quality is low; NICE advises against surgical sperm retrieval in that situation (1.27.1) and against supplements, antioxidants or medical treatments to improve sperm DNA integrity (1.24.6). ESHRE (add-ons) describes a meta-analysis of 4 observational studies with a higher pregnancy rate using testicular sperm, but of moderate quality and with confounding. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: What do NICE and AUA/ASRM say about ordering sperm DNA fragmentation, and in which context does AUA/ASRM contemplate it?
items.pearl: If the test will not change what you do with the couple, do not order it; if you contemplate it for recurrent loss or ART failures, explain that it is a specialist decision.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: NICE 2026 and ESHRE 2023 (unexplained infertility) against (very low certainty); AUA/ASRM against in the initial evaluation (moderate, C) and in favour in recurrent loss (moderate, C); ESHRE RPL 2022: could be considered (conditional). The guidelines disagree on the use of testicular sperm.

items.stem: Diego’s second semen analysis (3 months later) confirms a concentration of 8 × 10⁶/ml, with no azoospermia and no impaired libido. What is most appropriate now?

options.text: Physical examination of the scrotum and testes and consider serum testosterone and gonadotrophins.
options.why: Correct: NICE offers examination with 2 or more abnormal semen analyses and suggests considering testosterone and gonadotrophins (1.17.5); AUA/ASRM asks for FSH and testosterone in oligozoospermia.

options.text: Karyotype and Y microdeletion testing up front in every man with oligozoospermia.
options.why: At 8 × 10⁶/ml the thresholds are not met: Y microdeletion is for azoospermia or ≤1 million/ml (AUA/ASRM) or <1 million/ml (NICE), and karyotype for <5 million/ml.

options.text: Routine scrotal and transrectal ultrasound to complete the work-up.
options.why: AUA/ASRM advises against routine scrotal ultrasound and against TRUS/pelvic MRI in the initial evaluation.

options.text: Diagnostic testicular biopsy to decide whether it is obstructive or secretory.
options.why: AUA/ASRM does not recommend routine diagnostic biopsy, and the obstructive/non-obstructive distinction concerns azoospermia, which Diego does not have.

items.explanation: After confirming the abnormality, the next step is clinical and laboratory, low-cost and with expected yield; genetics, imaging and biopsy are reserved for specific indications.

items.stem: Diego has a palpable left varicocele, two abnormal semen analyses (without azoospermia), and they want to conceive spontaneously; Carla has no known factor. They ask what benefit to expect from repair. Which answer best fits the evidence?

options.text: Guidelines contemplate repair; estimated pregnancy rates are higher with repair, but they come largely from non-randomised studies and live-birth data are scarce.
options.why: Correct: AUA/ASRM (moderate; B) and NICE (consider) support repair in this profile, and both flag the limitations: non-randomised studies and selective reporting (AUA/ASRM) and few live-birth studies with mixed results (NICE).

options.text: Repairing the varicocele guarantees spontaneous pregnancy, so Carla no longer needs evaluation.
options.why: Nothing in the guidelines indicates a guarantee; NICE requires taking female factors into account and AUA/ASRM recommends evaluating both partners concurrently.

options.text: Repair is indicated even if it were only seen on ultrasound and not palpable.
options.why: AUA/ASRM strongly advises against repairing non-palpable varicoceles detected only by imaging; moreover Diego has a palpable one.

options.text: Repair is only indicated if there is non-obstructive azoospermia.
options.why: AUA/ASRM excludes azoospermia from the indication for varicocelectomy and only asks to inform that there is no definitive evidence in non-obstructive azoospermia.

items.explanation: Repair of a clinical varicocele has a defined indication and moderate support; present the benefit as an estimate with uncertainty, not as a promise.

items.stem: A 38-year-old man using long-acting injectable testosterone for “low energy” consults with his partner for infertility. His semen analysis shows azoospermia. What is the correct counselling?

options.text: Exogenous testosterone suppresses gonadotrophins and spermatogenesis; it should not be prescribed to someone seeking fertility, and recovery after stopping usually occurs although it may take months or, rarely, years.
options.why: Correct: matches the AUA/ASRM clinical principle and its description of the mechanism and recovery; NICE advises against androgens for semen abnormalities.

options.text: Increase the dose, because more testosterone stimulates testicular sperm production.
options.why: Exogenous testosterone causes negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary and reduces spermatogenesis; it does not stimulate it.

options.text: Switch to a nasal formulation, which has already been shown to be safe for fertility in the long term.
options.why: AUA/ASRM cites only two studies with preserved spermatogenesis, notes the lack of long-term data and advises against routine use in those trying to conceive.

options.text: Keep the testosterone and add an antioxidant to protect the sperm.
options.why: No guideline supports an antioxidant to counteract testosterone suppression; AUA/ASRM considers the usefulness of supplements in male infertility questionable.

items.explanation: Asking about testosterone (and other anabolic agents) is part of the history; it is a frequently reversible and preventable cause of azoospermia.

items.stem: Diego has two abnormal semen analyses and asks whether sperm DNA fragmentation “will decide whether ICSI is needed”. Which statement correctly reflects the guidelines?

options.text: NICE advises against it, AUA/ASRM does not recommend it in the initial evaluation and the ESHRE add-ons document sees insufficient evidence to use it to guide treatment.
options.why: Correct: summarises NICE 1.17.6, AUA/ASRM (moderate; C) and the ESHRE add-ons conclusion.

options.text: AUA/ASRM recommends it for every man with an abnormal semen analysis to choose the technique.
options.why: AUA/ASRM advises against it in the initial evaluation; it only contemplates it in specific contexts such as recurrent loss or repeated IVF failures.

options.text: NICE proposes doing it and treating an elevated result with antioxidants.
options.why: NICE advises against doing it (1.17.6) and against offering supplements, antioxidants or medical treatments to improve sperm DNA integrity (1.24.6).

options.text: ESHRE recommends it with solid evidence because the assays are interchangeable and standardised.
options.why: ESHRE emphasises the opposite: assays are not interchangeable and their thresholds are not standardised.

items.explanation: In the initial evaluation, none of the guidelines reviewed endorses fragmentation as a routine test; its nuances (recurrent loss, ART failures) are specialist indications.

items.title: Antioxidants and supplements in men: what the guidelines say
items.core: AUA/ASRM advises counselling that the benefits of supplements (for example antioxidants and vitamins) are of questionable clinical utility and that data do not allow recommending specific agents (moderate; grade B). ESHRE considers that adjunct oral antioxidants in men receiving fertility treatment are probably not recommended in unexplained infertility (conditional), and its add-ons document does not recommend them in ART. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
AUA/ASRM: there are no clear, reliable data on the various supplements; current data suggest they are likely not harmful, but it is questionable whether they provide tangible improvements in fertility outcomes. It cites a 2020 NIH Reproductive Medicine Network trial (174 men) that did not show an adequate effect on semen parameters or DNA integrity in the screening arm to proceed to full accrual, and a second 2020 RCT of folic acid and zinc in nearly 2400 men from infertile couples with no significant changes in semen quality or live births. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

ESHRE (unexplained infertility): the justification refers to low-quality evidence that does not show a benefit of antioxidants in men or women with unexplained infertility and adds that, although they are usually inexpensive, their benefit was not demonstrated. The study cited for that analysis is a review of couples with unexplained infertility with only 2 RCTs and 133 women, that is, there are very few direct data in men. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

ESHRE (add-ons): antioxidants are not recommended in ART and lack substantial and reliable evidence of a significant enhancement in live birth. The studies that tried to identify subgroups of patients who might benefit (by BMI, smoking, lifestyle factors, baseline DNA fragmentation, varicocele, etc.) were mostly small and retrospective, used various combinations of antioxidants, and used semen parameters or DNA fragmentation as surrogates rather than pregnancy rate. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

NICE (1.24.6) is more specific: do not offer supplements, antioxidants or medical treatments to improve sperm DNA integrity; the committee found no standardised treatment and no convincing benefit in live birth, clinical pregnancy, miscarriage, stillbirth or embryo quality. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What does AUA/ASRM state about supplements in male infertility, and what specific recommendation does NICE make (1.24.6)?
items.pearl: The four sources agree on not recommending a specific agent, but they do not say the same thing: distinguish “not recommended” from “harmful”.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: AUA/ASRM moderate (B) in favour of counselling that utility is questionable; ESHRE 2023 conditional; ESHRE add-ons and NICE 2026 against using them as adjuncts or for DNA integrity.

items.title: Cochrane 2022: how to read the male antioxidant result
items.core: The Cochrane review (90 RCTs; 10,303 subfertile men) found a possible increase in live birth (OR 1.43; 95% CI 1.07–1.91; 12 RCTs; 1283 men; very low certainty) that is no longer significant when high risk-of-bias studies are excluded (Peto OR 1.22; 95% CI 0.85–1.75; 8 RCTs; 827 men); the authors conclude the overall evidence is inconclusive. [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
Other results of the review: clinical pregnancy OR 1.89 (95% CI 1.45–2.47; 20 RCTs; 1706 men; low certainty); miscarriage no difference (OR 1.46; 95% CI 0.75–2.83; 6 RCTs; very low certainty); mild gastrointestinal discomfort OR 2.70 (95% CI 1.46–4.99; 16 RCTs; low certainty). Assuming a 16% baseline live birth, the review estimates 17% to 27% with antioxidants, but from only 246 live births in 12 small or medium-sized studies. [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]]

Stated limitations: of 67 studies included in the meta-analysis, only 20 reported clinical pregnancy and 12 live birth; 20 different antioxidants were compared and no conclusions could be drawn between them; the review excluded men with idiopathic infertility and normal semen parameters, so it does not apply to them. [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]]

How it fits with the guidelines: ESHRE (add-ons) reproduces the same live-birth figures and concludes that antioxidants lack substantial and reliable evidence of a significant enhancement in live birth; AUA/ASRM considers the data inadequate to recommend specific agents, and NICE advises against offering them to improve sperm DNA integrity (1.24.6). There is no false equivalence between Cochrane and the guidelines: Cochrane does not demonstrate efficacy (very low certainty and no significant effect after excluding high risk-of-bias studies) and the guidelines do not claim they are harmful. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What happens to the live-birth effect in the Cochrane review when high risk-of-bias studies are excluded?
items.application: If someone quotes “OR 1.43”, ask about certainty, the analysis without high bias, and whether the outcome is live birth or a semen parameter.

evidence.label: limited
evidence.note: Cochrane 2022: very low to low certainty, overall evidence inconclusive; ESHRE add-ons 2023 and AUA/ASRM do not recommend specific agents.

items.title: What to tell the man who wants to take “something” to improve his semen
items.core: A message that fits the sources: the usefulness of supplements is questionable and there is no agent to recommend (AUA/ASRM); antioxidants are not recommended as adjuncts in ART (ESHRE); in the Cochrane review they may cause mild gastrointestinal discomfort; and habits (alcohol, smoking, weight, scrotal temperature) have their own NICE advice. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
On habits, NICE advises informing men that excessive alcohol intake is detrimental to semen quality and that drinking within the UK low-risk limits (14 units per week, spread across several days) is unlikely to affect it; that smoking is associated with reduced semen quality (although the impact on fertility is uncertain) and stopping improves general health; that a BMI ≥30 kg/m² carries an increased risk of reduced fertility; that elevated scrotal temperature is associated with reduced semen quality but it is uncertain whether loose-fitting underwear improves fertility; and that there is no consistent evidence of an association between caffeine and fertility problems. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

AUA/ASRM allows discussing risk factors (lifestyle, medication, environmental and occupational exposures) but advises saying that data on most of them are limited (conditional; grade C). [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

If he decides to take an antioxidant anyway, the honest message is that current data suggest it is probably not harmful (AUA/ASRM), that it may cause mild gastrointestinal discomfort (Cochrane, low certainty), and that no product or dose is supported; the decision is shared and should not delay the rest of the couple’s work-up and treatment. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]]
items.recall: Which four messages on supplements and habits would you give a man who asks for “something” to improve his semen?
items.application: Possible phrase: “I cannot promise that a supplement will improve your chances of having a baby; I can help with what is supported: reviewing habits and moving forward with the work-up for both of you”.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: Habit advice: NICE 2004/2013 (updated 2026), certainty not graded; supplements: AUA/ASRM moderate (B), Cochrane low to very low certainty.

items.stem: Diego reads that the 2022 Cochrane review “shows” that antioxidants increase live births (OR 1.43). He asks you to confirm it. What is the correct reading?

options.text: It is a very low-certainty result (12 RCTs, 1283 men) that does not hold when high risk-of-bias studies are excluded (Peto OR 1.22; 95% CI 0.85–1.75); the authors consider the evidence inconclusive.
options.why: Correct: matches the Cochrane abstract and its reproduction in ESHRE (add-ons).

options.text: It is a high-certainty result confirming that antioxidants increase live births, and the guidelines ignore it.
options.why: Certainty is very low, and ESHRE (add-ons) discusses this very review to conclude there is no substantial, reliable evidence.

options.text: It also confirms that antioxidants reduce miscarriage.
options.why: The review found no difference in miscarriage (OR 1.46; 95% CI 0.75–2.83; very low certainty).

options.text: It shows they have no adverse effects.
options.why: The review found more mild gastrointestinal discomfort with antioxidants (OR 2.70; 95% CI 1.46–4.99; low certainty).

items.explanation: An isolated OR with an interval excluding 1 is not proof: certainty, risk of bias and the sensitivity analysis matter.

items.stem: After the conversation, Diego says he wants to try an antioxidant supplement anyway. Which approach is consistent with the sources?

options.text: Shared decision: explain that utility is questionable and no agent or dose is supported, that data suggest it is probably not harmful although it may cause mild digestive discomfort, and do not delay the rest of the work-up and treatment.
options.why: Correct: reflects AUA/ASRM (questionable utility, probably not harmful, no specific agent) and Cochrane (mild gastrointestinal discomfort, low certainty).

options.text: Prescribe several antioxidants at high doses “to be safe”, because more is better.
options.why: No source supports a specific agent or dose or that combining more is better; Cochrane could not draw conclusions when comparing antioxidants with each other.

options.text: Forbid it, because Cochrane showed serious harm.
options.why: Cochrane describes mild gastrointestinal discomfort, not serious harm, and AUA/ASRM states they are probably not harmful.

options.text: Promise that this way they will avoid assisted reproduction.
options.why: There is no reliable evidence of an effect on pregnancy or live birth; AUA/ASRM, ESHRE and NICE do not support that promise.

items.explanation: The decision belongs to the informed patient: your role is not to over-promise, not to alarm, and not to let the supplement delay what is supported.

items.stem: A leaflet states that a supplement “improved concentration and motility in a study of 40 men”. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: It describes a change in semen parameters (surrogate outcomes); by itself it does not show more pregnancies or live births.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE (add-ons) notes that the studies looking for subgroups who might benefit used semen parameters or DNA fragmentation as surrogates rather than pregnancy rate, and Cochrane reports that few studies reported pregnancy (20 of 67) or live birth (12).

options.text: It means the supplement increases the chance of live birth.
options.why: A change in parameters is not the same as live birth; guidelines do not recommend them precisely because of the lack of evidence on those outcomes.

options.text: It means the evidence is high quality because 40 men is a sufficient sample.
options.why: A study of 40 men is small and is not high-quality evidence: ESHRE (add-ons) notes that the subgroup studies of antioxidants were mostly small and retrospective, and Cochrane rates the certainty as low to very low.

options.text: It means it is safe, because no adverse effects are mentioned.
options.why: Absence of mention does not prove safety; the Cochrane review did record mild gastrointestinal discomfort with antioxidants.

items.explanation: Semen parameters, pregnancy and live birth are three different outcomes: improvement in the first does not automatically translate into the others.

items.stem: According to the AUA/ASRM guideline, approximately how often is a male factor the sole cause or a contributing factor in infertile couples?

options.text: Sole cause in about 5% and contributing in another 10%.
options.why: This greatly underestimates the AUA/ASRM figures (20% and 30–40%).

options.text: Sole cause in about 60% and contributing in another 30%.
options.why: This overestimates the proportion in which it is the sole cause (about 20%).

options.text: It is never the sole cause; it only contributes.
options.why: AUA/ASRM estimates that it is the sole cause in about 20% of couples.

options.text: Sole cause in about 20% and contributing in another 30–40%.
options.why: Correct: this is the AUA/ASRM estimate, which acknowledges that the true prevalence is not well defined because of differing definitions and populations.

items.explanation: This is why AUA/ASRM recommends assessing both partners concurrently: without an adequate male evaluation, the woman may receive unnecessary, costly or invasive treatment.

items.stem: He brings a “normal” result from a home semen test bought online and asks whether that is enough. According to AUA/ASRM, what do you answer?

options.text: It does not replace a semen analysis in a specialised andrology laboratory: its accuracy varies and results cannot be extrapolated from one test to another.
options.why: Correct: this is the AUA/ASRM warning about home or mail-in kits.

options.text: Yes, it is enough if the test carries a CE mark.
options.why: AUA/ASRM makes no such exception: home kits do not replace the andrology laboratory.

options.text: Yes, it is enough for concentration, though not for morphology.
options.why: AUA/ASRM warns that their accuracy varies; it does not accept them as a substitute for any parameter.

options.text: Repeating the same home test after 3 months is enough.
options.why: Repeating a non-validated test does not solve the problem: the semen analysis should be done in a specialised laboratory.

items.explanation: The man's initial evaluation includes a reproductive history and one or more semen analyses (AUA/ASRM: strong; grade B), done in an andrology laboratory.

items.stem: A couple trying for 13 months, with no known cause. The gynaecologist plans to complete her work-up first (ultrasound, HSG) and order the semen analysis only if everything is normal. What is appropriate?

options.text: Keep the plan: the semen analysis is the last step of the work-up.
options.why: The guidelines do not position the semen analysis as the last step; it is ordered alongside her work-up.

options.text: Wait until 2 years before assessing the man.
options.why: NICE offers assessment of both partners after 1 year with no known cause.

options.text: Assess both partners at the same time and order the semen analysis now.
options.why: Correct: AUA/ASRM recommends concurrent assessment of both partners (expert opinion), and NICE offers assessment of both after 1 year (1.16.5).

options.text: Order only male hormones, which are cheaper than a semen analysis.
options.why: Semen analysis is part of the initial evaluation (strong; grade B); hormones are not first line for everyone.

items.explanation: Order the semen analysis at the same visit as her tests: leaving it to the end may expose her to unnecessary tests or treatment.

items.stem: Which set of values matches the reference limits (5th centile) in the WHO manual, 6th edition (2021)?

options.text: Concentration 16 × 10⁶/ml; total number 39 × 10⁶; progressive motility 42%; normal forms 4%.
options.why: 42% is total motility; progressive motility is 30%.

options.text: Concentration 20 × 10⁶/ml; total number 40 × 10⁶; progressive motility 50%; normal forms 14%.
options.why: None of these values matches the 6th edition.

options.text: Concentration 16 × 10⁶/ml; total number 39 × 10⁶; progressive motility 30%; normal forms 4%.
options.why: Correct: these are the values in Table 8.3 of the manual (also: volume 1.4 ml, total motility 42%, vitality 54%).

options.text: Concentration 10 × 10⁶/ml; total number 20 × 10⁶; progressive motility 20%; normal forms 1%.
options.why: These are invented values, well below the WHO limits.

items.explanation: 5th centile of about 3500 men in 12 countries whose partners conceived within ≤12 months: volume 1.4 ml; 16 × 10⁶/ml; 39 × 10⁶; total motility 42%; progressive 30%; vitality 54%; normal forms 4%.

items.stem: What exactly do the reference limits in the WHO manual (6th edition) represent?

options.text: The 5th centile of men whose partners conceived naturally within ≤12 months; it is not a limit between fertile and infertile men.
options.why: Correct: the manual stresses the overlap between groups, fertility as a continuum, and that it is not a guideline for clinical decisions.

options.text: The minimum needed to be fertile.
options.why: The manual explicitly states that the 5th centile does not separate fertile from infertile men.

options.text: The 5th centile of men attending infertility clinics.
options.why: The reference population excluded men attending infertility clinics.

options.text: The threshold below which ICSI is indicated.
options.why: The manual is not a clinical decision guideline and sets no treatment indications.

items.explanation: Teach each figure with its full name: “5th centile of men whose partner conceived within ≤12 months”, not “minimum to be fertile”.

items.stem: A semen analysis shows a concentration of 15.5 × 10⁶/ml (other parameters normal). How does it compare with the WHO 6th-edition references and the AUA/ASRM tables?

options.text: Normal by both references.
options.why: 15.5 falls below the 6th-edition 5th centile (16 × 10⁶/ml).

options.text: Oligozoospermia by both references.
options.why: In the AUA/ASRM example (Figure 1) oligozoospermia is <15 million/ml; 15.5 is not.

options.text: A diagnosis of male infertility, because it is below the 5th centile.
options.why: The 5th centile does not separate fertile from infertile men; an isolated value is repeated and interpreted in context.

options.text: Below the WHO 6th-edition 5th centile (16 × 10⁶/ml), but not below the <15 million/ml that AUA/ASRM uses in its example (Figure 1), taken from the 5th edition.
options.why: Correct: AUA/ASRM cites the 6th edition in its text, but refers to the “WHO 5” limits and defines oligozoospermia as <15 million/ml in its Figure 1 (5th-edition values).

items.explanation: Check which edition each source uses: the 15 versus 16 × 10⁶/ml difference can change the label, not the prognosis.

items.stem: According to AUA/ASRM, in which of these findings does the semen analysis precisely distinguish an infertile man?

options.text: A concentration of 14 × 10⁶/ml.
options.why: An isolated value slightly below the limit does not by itself predict infertility.

options.text: Azoospermia.
options.why: Correct: except in azoospermia and some extreme pictures (complete globozoospermia, necrozoospermia, complete asthenozoospermia), semen analysis does not distinguish precisely.

options.text: Normal forms of 3%.
options.why: Morphology has limited prognostic value, according to WHO.

options.text: Progressive motility of 28%.
options.why: One isolated, slightly low parameter is not predictive for the individual.

items.explanation: Semen parameters are highly variable: they are assessed together, and the more fall below the limit, the greater the probability of subfertility, without being predictive for the individual.

items.stem: An otherwise normal semen analysis reports 3% normal forms. The couple has read that this means “we need ICSI”. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Explain that morphology has limited prognostic value and that an isolated value is interpreted as a whole and in context.
options.why: Correct: WHO notes its limited prognostic value and that distinguishing 3% from 5% in an individual requires assessing 1500 spermatozoa by highly trained staff.

options.text: Confirm that ICSI is indicated.
options.why: An isolated morphology value neither confirms infertility nor indicates ICSI by itself.

options.text: Diagnose male infertility and rule out spontaneous pregnancy.
options.why: Some men with abnormal parameters conceive naturally; semen analysis is not predictive for the individual.

options.text: Start antioxidants until morphology normalises.
options.why: No source supports a specific agent, and changing a semen parameter is a surrogate outcome.

items.explanation: Faced with one isolated, slightly low value: look at the whole picture, repeat and put it in context before giving a verdict.

items.stem: Which of these statements about a “normal” semen analysis is correct according to AUA/ASRM and WHO?

options.text: It guarantees the man's fertility.
options.why: Semen analysis does not precisely distinguish fertile from infertile men except in extreme pictures.

options.text: It can hide sperm that do not function well; this is why AUA/ASRM evaluates the man after failed assisted reproduction cycles or recurrent pregnancy loss.
options.why: Correct: in those situations AUA/ASRM proposes considering karyotype and sperm DNA fragmentation testing.

options.text: It excludes the couple from being classified as infertile.
options.why: WHO notes that some men with a normal ejaculate are classed as infertile, mainly because of female factors.

options.text: It makes any future physical examination unnecessary.
options.why: AUA/ASRM notes that 1–6% of men evaluated for infertility have undiagnosed medical disease at that time, which is why physical examination is part of the evaluation.

items.explanation: “Within range” is not the same as “fertile”: semen analysis informs, but does not predict on its own.

items.stem: A semen sample was collected after 12 days of abstinence and reached the laboratory 2 hours later. How do you assess it according to WHO?

options.text: Valid, because long abstinence only improves concentration.
options.why: Abstinence exceeds WHO's 7 days and the delay exceeds 60 minutes.

options.text: Valid if the sample was kept refrigerated.
options.why: WHO does not contemplate refrigeration as a fix; the problem is abstinence and time to analysis.

options.text: Valid only for morphology.
options.why: The sample does not meet WHO conditions; the appropriate step is to repeat it.

options.text: Outside pre-analytical conditions: repeat it with 2–7 days of abstinence and analysis ideally within 30 minutes (60 at most).
options.why: Correct: these are WHO's requirements for collection and analysis.

items.explanation: Before interpreting or repeating “just in case”, ask about abstinence, lost fractions, the container used and time to the laboratory.

items.stem: He asks whether he can collect the sample at home using an ordinary latex condom during intercourse. What does WHO advise?

options.text: Yes, as long as he adds lubricant.
options.why: Lubricants are avoided unless validated as non-spermatotoxic.

options.text: Yes, if he delivers it within 3 hours.
options.why: Besides the condom, WHO asks for analysis ideally within 30 minutes (60 at most).

options.text: No: ordinary latex condoms contain agents that interfere with motility.
options.why: Correct: WHO advises against them and against lubricants unless validated as non-spermatotoxic.

options.text: Yes, it is the method of choice because it avoids losing the first fraction.
options.why: WHO recommends collection in a private room close to the laboratory, not with an ordinary condom.

items.explanation: A complete sample, without ordinary latex condoms or non-validated lubricants, and in a room close to the laboratory when possible.

items.stem: A man with a normal semen analysis plans to abstain for 10 days before the fertile window “to build up sperm”. What do the data reported by ASRM (2022) say?

options.text: It is advisable: the longer the abstinence, the better the fertility.
options.why: The data cited by ASRM point the other way beyond 5–10 days.

options.text: Daily ejaculation lowers concentration below normal in all men.
options.why: In men with normal semen quality, concentration and motility remained normal with daily ejaculation.

options.text: This has been shown in randomised trials.
options.why: The ASRM data on abstinence are observational and retrospective.

options.text: Abstinence intervals longer than 5 days may adversely affect counts, and from 10 days parameters begin to deteriorate.
options.why: Correct: ASRM notes that abstinence intervals longer than 5 days may adversely affect sperm counts and that, from 10 days or more, semen parameters begin to deteriorate; as little as 2 days is already associated with normal densities.

items.explanation: ASRM notes that 2 days of abstinence are already associated with normal densities; the data are observational.

items.stem: After a first semen analysis below the reference limit, what interval for repeating it do the guidelines propose?

options.text: All three guidelines propose repeating it after 2 weeks.
options.why: None proposes 2 weeks: 3 months (ESHRE, NICE) and one month (AUA/ASRM).

options.text: AUA/ASRM proposes 3 months; ESHRE and NICE, one month.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.text: ESHRE recommends repeating it after 3 months and NICE ideally at 3 months; AUA/ASRM proposes considering at least two analyses a month apart.
options.why: Correct: the difference in interval is real; what they share is not deciding on a single abnormal result.

options.text: No guideline recommends repeating it: one abnormal result is enough to decide.
options.why: All three agree on not deciding on a single abnormal result.

items.explanation: NICE justifies 3 months by the length of the sperm formation cycle; AUA/ASRM bases its advice on biological variability.

items.stem: A man's first semen analysis shows azoospermia. According to NICE NG257, when should the confirmatory test be done?

options.text: Ideally at 3 months, like any other abnormal result.
options.why: The 3-month interval is the general one (1.17.4); with azoospermia, the same recommendation asks for it to be brought forward.

options.text: As soon as possible.
options.why: Correct: with a gross deficiency (azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia), NICE advises repeating it as soon as possible (1.17.4).

options.text: There is no need to repeat it: proceed directly to surgical sperm retrieval.
options.why: NICE always offers a confirmatory test.

options.text: After 1 year.
options.why: No guideline proposes waiting a year; with azoospermia, NICE asks to repeat it as soon as possible.

items.explanation: NICE: confirmatory repeat ideally at 3 months, but as soon as possible with azoospermia or severe oligozoospermia.

items.stem: In which of these men does AUA/ASRM indicate hormonal evaluation with FSH and testosterone?

options.text: A man with atrophic testes on examination.
options.why: Correct: AUA/ASRM asks for it with impaired libido, erectile dysfunction, oligozoospermia or azoospermia, atrophic testes or signs of a hormonal abnormality (expert opinion).

options.text: Every man at the first visit, before the semen analysis.
options.why: AUA/ASRM does not consider endocrine evaluation a first-line test for every man.

options.text: An asymptomatic man with a normal semen analysis in a couple with unexplained infertility.
options.why: None of the indications applies, and ESHRE does not recommend serum hormones with a normal semen analysis (strong).

options.text: A man with a normal semen analysis who wants to “know his level” of testosterone.
options.why: Curiosity is not one of the AUA/ASRM clinical indications.

items.explanation: Hormonal evaluation is indicated by clinical findings or the semen analysis (suggested in oligozoospermia, particularly <10 million/ml), not routinely.

items.stem: In a man with oligozoospermia, fasting total testosterone drawn at 9 a.m. is 250 ng/dL. According to AUA/ASRM, what comes next?

options.text: Start exogenous testosterone to normalise it.
options.why: AUA/ASRM states that exogenous testosterone should not be prescribed to men seeking current or future fertility.

options.text: Repeat it together with free or bioavailable testosterone, LH, estradiol and prolactin.
options.why: Correct: with low total testosterone (<300 ng/dL), AUA/ASRM asks to repeat it with that panel.

options.text: Consider it normal, because it is above 200 ng/dL.
options.why: The cut-off AUA/ASRM uses is <300 ng/dL.

options.text: Discard the result because it should be drawn in the afternoon.
options.why: AUA/ASRM advises drawing it in the morning (8–10 a.m.), as was done.

items.explanation: Testosterone in the morning (8–10 a.m.) and fasting; if low, repeat with free or bioavailable testosterone, LH, estradiol and prolactin before labelling.

items.stem: In the history of the male partner of an infertile couple, what does NICE explicitly recommend asking about?

options.text: Only prescribed drugs; gym products are not relevant.
options.why: NICE explicitly includes products such as anabolic steroids.

options.text: Nothing about drugs if the semen analysis is normal.
options.why: The question about drugs and products is part of the history, whatever the semen analysis shows.

options.text: Only a family history of infertility.
options.why: NICE explicitly asks about drugs and other products.

options.text: Drugs and other products that can affect fertility, such as testosterone-replacement therapy, finasteride, anabolic steroids or cannabis.
options.why: Correct: this is NICE recommendation 1.13.1.

items.explanation: Record everything the man takes, including “boosters” and gym products, before ordering hormones.

items.stem: An azoospermic man has a semen volume of 0.8 ml with acidic pH, normal serum testosterone and palpable vasa deferentia. According to AUA/ASRM, which imaging test is justified?

options.text: Transrectal ultrasound or pelvic MRI, for suspected ejaculatory duct obstruction.
options.why: Correct: AUA/ASRM reserves these tests for this profile: acidic, azoospermic semen, volume <1.4 ml, normal testosterone and palpable vasa.

options.text: Diagnostic testicular biopsy to distinguish obstructive from non-obstructive azoospermia.
options.why: AUA/ASRM advises against diagnostic testicular biopsy for that purpose (expert opinion).

options.text: Renal ultrasound, for vasal agenesis.
options.why: Renal ultrasound is recommended in vasal agenesis, but here the vasa are palpable.

options.text: None: imaging is never indicated in male infertility.
options.why: AUA/ASRM advises against routine imaging, not imaging aimed at a specific clinical question.

items.explanation: An imaging test is ordered for a specific clinical question, not to “complete” the work-up.

items.stem: In the initial evaluation of a man with obesity and a highly contracted dartos, scrotal examination is difficult. What does AUA/ASRM say about scrotal ultrasound?

options.text: It is indicated routinely in every infertile man.
options.why: AUA/ASRM advises against routine scrotal ultrasound in the initial evaluation (expert opinion).

options.text: It should never be done, because non-palpable varicoceles are not treated.
options.why: That non-palpable varicoceles are not treated justifies not doing it routinely, not banning it when examination is difficult.

options.text: It is not routine, but it can be used when examination is difficult, as in this case.
options.why: Correct: AUA/ASRM contemplates it if examination is difficult, to confirm a varicocele before repair, or to assess treatment success.

options.text: It should be replaced by pelvic MRI.
options.why: AUA/ASRM reserves pelvic MRI for suspected ejaculatory duct obstruction.

items.explanation: “Not routinely” is not “never”: scrotal ultrasound answers specific questions.

items.stem: An infertile man has an isolated, small, reducible right varicocele. What does AUA/ASRM say about abdominal imaging?

options.text: Always, because every right varicocele suggests a retroperitoneal tumour.
options.why: AUA/ASRM does not recommend routine imaging for an isolated small or moderate right varicocele.

options.text: Never, whatever the size or course.
options.why: AUA/ASRM does recommend considering it for a new-onset or non-reducible varicocele, especially if large.

options.text: It is not recommended routinely; it is considered for a new-onset or non-reducible varicocele, especially if large.
options.why: Correct: a retrospective study of more than 4000 men with varicocele found no difference in cancer diagnoses by laterality.

options.text: Only if the semen analysis is normal.
options.why: The AUA/ASRM criterion is based on the varicocele's features, not on the semen analysis.

items.explanation: Laterality alone is not an indication for abdominal imaging; new onset, non-reducibility or large size do make it worth considering.

items.stem: A man with primary infertility, a persistent concentration of 3 × 10⁶/ml, elevated FSH and small testes. Which genetic tests fit AUA/ASRM and NICE?

options.text: Karyotype (AUA/ASRM indicates it for <5 million/ml with elevated FSH; NICE suggests considering it); no Y microdeletion, because the concentration exceeds 1 million/ml.
options.why: Correct: Y microdeletion testing is reserved for ≤1 million/ml (AUA/ASRM) or <1 million/ml (NICE).

options.text: Karyotype and Y microdeletion, because it is below 5 million/ml.
options.why: The threshold for Y microdeletion is ≤1 (AUA/ASRM) or <1 million/ml (NICE), not 5.

options.text: CFTR only.
options.why: CFTR testing is reserved for vasal agenesis or idiopathic obstructive azoospermia.

options.text: None: genetic tests are only done in azoospermia.
options.why: Both guidelines contemplate karyotype below 5 million/ml (AUA/ASRM with elevated FSH, atrophy or impaired production).

items.explanation: Before ordering genetics, check the concentration, whether it is persistent and whether FSH is elevated or there is atrophy: the indication depends on the guideline.

items.stem: A man with non-obstructive azoospermia has an AZFb Y-chromosome microdeletion. According to NICE NG257, what is appropriate regarding surgical sperm retrieval?

options.text: Offer it as in any non-obstructive azoospermia.
options.why: NICE makes an explicit exception for AZFa and AZFb microdeletions.

options.text: Offer it only after repairing a varicocele.
options.why: That is not NICE's criterion; the problem is the AZFb microdeletion.

options.text: Do not offer it, as with an AZFc microdeletion.
options.why: According to the NICE committee, AZFc does not affect retrieval success.

options.text: Do not offer it, because its success is very low with AZFa or AZFb microdeletions.
options.why: Correct: NICE advises not offering it (1.26.1); the committee notes that an AZFc microdeletion does not affect retrieval success.

items.explanation: The microdeletion region matters: AZFa/AZFb, very low retrieval success; AZFc, no effect on success. With a specific genetic defect, NICE offers genetic counselling.

items.stem: An azoospermic man with vasal agenesis. According to AUA/ASRM, which genetic testing applies?

options.text: Y microdeletion only.
options.why: Y microdeletion testing targets impaired production, not absence of the vas.

options.text: CFTR (including the 5T allele) in him, and genetic evaluation of his partner.
options.why: Correct: AUA/ASRM asks for CFTR in vasal agenesis and partner evaluation if he is a carrier or has no vas (expert opinion); NICE also contemplates CFTR with a vasal abnormality.

options.text: None: the cause is anatomical, not genetic.
options.why: Vasal agenesis is precisely an indication for CFTR testing.

options.text: CFTR in him, with no implications for his partner.
options.why: AUA/ASRM asks for genetic evaluation of the partner in this situation.

items.explanation: In vasal agenesis, AUA/ASRM also recommends renal ultrasound.

items.stem: A man with an abnormal semen analysis and a non-palpable left varicocele seen only on ultrasound. According to AUA/ASRM, is varicocelectomy indicated?

options.text: No: AUA/ASRM does not recommend repairing non-palpable varicoceles detected only by imaging (strong; grade C).
options.why: Correct: treating them is not associated with improved semen parameters or fertility rates.

options.text: Yes, because the semen analysis is abnormal (moderate; grade B).
options.why: The moderate recommendation (grade B) requires a palpable varicocele.

options.text: Yes, if it is left-sided, because 85% are.
options.why: Laterality does not change the indication; what counts is that it is palpable.

options.text: Only if the couple is going to have IVF.
options.why: The recommendation against repairing non-palpable varicoceles does not depend on the reproductive technique.

items.explanation: Palpable + infertility + abnormal parameters (without azoospermia): repair is considered. Seen only on ultrasound: not repaired.

items.stem: A couple is about to start assisted reproduction and he has a clinical varicocele. What do AUA/ASRM and NICE say about repairing it first?

options.text: Both recommend it based on RCT evidence.
options.why: NICE identified no RCTs on treating varicocele before assisted conception.

options.text: AUA/ASRM cites a meta-analysis of 7 retrospective non-randomised studies with 1.76-fold higher odds of pregnancy and live birth; NICE found no RCTs and makes no recommendation for that population.
options.why: Correct: this is a genuine difference between guidelines, based on non-randomised evidence.

options.text: NICE explicitly advises against it before IVF.
options.why: NICE makes no recommendation for that population; it does not advise against it.

options.text: AUA/ASRM advises against it and NICE recommends it.
options.why: That is not the case: AUA/ASRM describes a possible benefit and NICE makes no recommendation.

items.explanation: “Makes no recommendation” does not equal “advises against”: NICE's recommendation addresses couples trying to conceive spontaneously.

items.stem: A man with non-obstructive azoospermia and a palpable varicocele, about to undergo sperm retrieval. What should he be told according to AUA/ASRM?

options.text: That prior repair is mandatory.
options.why: AUA/ASRM does not require repair; it states that there is no definitive evidence supporting it.

options.text: That repair will certainly restore sperm to the ejaculate.
options.why: There is no definitive evidence of benefit in this situation.

options.text: That retrieval is contraindicated while he has a varicocele.
options.why: AUA/ASRM sets no such contraindication.

options.text: That there is no definitive evidence supporting varicocele repair before retrieval.
options.why: Correct: AUA/ASRM asks for this to be explained; moreover, its recommendation to consider varicocelectomy excludes azoospermia.

items.explanation: The AUA/ASRM recommendation to consider varicocelectomy (moderate; grade B) explicitly excludes azoospermia.

items.stem: A man with idiopathic infertility (no hypogonadotropic hypogonadism). How do NICE and AUA/ASRM differ on the use of hormonal treatments?

options.text: Both recommend clomiphene first line.
options.why: Neither recommends it first line; NICE leaves it to trials and AUA/ASRM notes limited benefits of SERMs.

options.text: Both allow androgens to improve the semen analysis.
options.why: NICE advises against androgens and AUA/ASRM against prescribing exogenous testosterone to men seeking fertility.

options.text: NICE reserves gonadotrophins or anti-oestrogens for clinical trials; AUA/ASRM allows considering an FSH analogue (conditional; grade B).
options.why: Correct: NICE 1.24.2 versus AUA/ASRM, which also notes that SERMs offer limited benefits relative to ART results (expert opinion).

options.text: NICE recommends gonadotrophins routinely; AUA/ASRM forbids them.
options.why: It is almost the opposite: NICE reserves them for trials and AUA/ASRM allows considering them.

items.explanation: Outside hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, the guidelines diverge: clinical trial only (NICE) versus conditional use (AUA/ASRM).

items.stem: A man with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism who wants to have children. What is appropriate according to NICE and AUA/ASRM?

options.text: Exogenous testosterone to correct the deficiency.
options.why: Exogenous testosterone suppresses gonadotrophins and spermatogenesis; it is not prescribed to men seeking fertility.

options.text: Antioxidants for 3 months.
options.why: They do not treat hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and no source supports a specific agent.

options.text: Only a clinical trial, as in idiopathic infertility.
options.why: NICE reserves trials for cases without hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; here it offers gonadotrophins.

options.text: Gonadotrophins (NICE), investigating the aetiology and treating according to the diagnosis (AUA/ASRM).
options.why: Correct: NICE offers gonadotrophins in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (1.24.1).
