items.explanation: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with a wish to conceive: gonadotrophins, not testosterone.

items.stem: A man with testosterone deficiency who wants children asks whether short-acting nasal testosterone “does not affect fertility”. What does AUA/ASRM say?

options.text: It is safe for fertility and the guideline recommends it.
options.why: This overstates the data: two studies, no long-term data and no routine recommendation.

options.text: It causes irreversible azoospermia in all cases.
options.why: Spermatogenesis was preserved in two studies; suppression is described with long-acting testosterone.

options.text: Spermatogenesis was preserved in two studies, but long-term data are lacking and the guideline does not advise it routinely.
options.why: Correct: this is the AUA/ASRM nuance on short-acting nasal testosterone.

options.text: It is equivalent to the long-acting form.
options.why: AUA/ASRM distinguishes them: the long-acting form suppresses the axis and can cause oligo- or azoospermia.

items.explanation: Long-acting testosterone suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary axis; recovery after stopping usually occurs, but may take months or, rarely, years.

items.stem: A couple with three pregnancy losses. What do AUA/ASRM and the ESHRE recurrent pregnancy loss guideline (2022) say about sperm DNA fragmentation testing?

options.text: Both advise against it, as in the initial evaluation.
options.why: In recurrent pregnancy loss, AUA/ASRM recommends it and ESHRE contemplates it.

options.text: AUA/ASRM recommends evaluating the man with fragmentation testing (moderate; grade C); ESHRE says it could be considered for diagnostic purposes using a validated test (conditional).
options.why: Correct: this is the scenario in which AUA/ASRM does recommend it, and ESHRE is more cautious.

options.text: ESHRE strongly recommends it; AUA/ASRM does not address it.
options.why: ESHRE uses a conditional recommendation (“could be considered”) and AUA/ASRM does address it, in favour.

options.text: Both recommend it only if the semen analysis is abnormal.
options.why: Neither makes the indication in this context conditional on an abnormal semen analysis.

items.explanation: With recurrent pregnancy loss, AUA/ASRM evaluates the man with karyotype (expert opinion) and fragmentation (moderate; C); ESHRE does not do parental karyotyping routinely, but after individual risk assessment.

items.stem: A non-azoospermic man with an elevated sperm DNA fragmentation index. What do the guidelines say about using testicular sperm?

options.text: AUA/ASRM says it may be considered (clinical principle); NICE advises against surgical sperm retrieval in that situation.
options.why: Correct: this is the point of greatest disagreement; ESHRE (add-ons) describes a meta-analysis of 4 observational studies with confounding.

options.text: The guidelines agree in recommending it.
options.why: NICE advises against it (1.27.1); AUA/ASRM only allows considering it.

options.text: NICE recommends it and AUA/ASRM advises against it.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.text: The guidelines agree on first treating with antioxidants to reduce fragmentation.
options.why: NICE advises against supplements, antioxidants or medical treatments to improve sperm DNA integrity (1.24.6).

items.explanation: There is no consensus on what to do with an elevated result: which is why the test should not be ordered if it will not change what you do with the couple.

items.stem: What reasons does NICE give for advising against sperm DNA fragmentation testing?

options.text: That high-quality RCTs showed it does not predict pregnancy.
options.why: NICE does not rely on RCTs showing this; ESHRE notes that no study has tested whether performing the test changes outcomes.

options.text: There is no effective treatment, the assays are expensive and take weeks, the link with subfertility has not been established, and it is unclear which test and threshold to use.
options.why: Correct: this is NICE's reasoning for recommendation 1.17.6.

options.text: That it is always normal if the semen analysis is normal.
options.why: That is not NICE's argument; WHO describes it as only partially related to semen quality.

options.text: That it is a dangerous test for the man.
options.why: No source claims a risk to the man; the problem is its usefulness.

items.explanation: ESHRE adds that assays are not interchangeable and thresholds are not standardised; AUA/ASRM agrees on the lack of prospective studies and on inconsistent cut-offs.

items.stem: What is the AUA/ASRM position on supplements (antioxidants, vitamins) in male infertility?

options.text: It recommends a specific antioxidant complex for 3 months.
options.why: AUA/ASRM considers that the data do not allow recommending specific agents.

options.text: It advises against them as harmful (strong).
options.why: AUA/ASRM states that data suggest they are likely not harmful.

options.text: It does not address them.
options.why: It does address them, with a moderate recommendation (grade B).

options.text: Counsel that their clinical utility is questionable and that the data do not allow recommending specific agents (moderate; grade B).
options.why: Correct: AUA/ASRM adds that they are likely not harmful, but that it is questionable whether they improve fertility outcomes.

items.explanation: Distinguish “not recommended” from “harmful”: the sources agree on not recommending a specific agent, not on their being harmful.

items.stem: What did the 2020 RCT of folic acid and zinc in nearly 2400 men from infertile couples, cited by AUA/ASRM, show?

options.text: No significant changes in semen quality or live births.
options.why: Correct: it is one of the two trials AUA/ASRM uses to question the usefulness of supplements.

options.text: More live births, with no change in semen parameters.
options.why: It showed no significant change in live births.

options.text: Better semen parameters, with no change in live births.
options.why: It showed no significant change in semen quality either.

options.text: More miscarriages with the supplement.
options.why: AUA/ASRM does not describe that result; it cites the trial for the absence of changes in semen quality and live births.

items.explanation: AUA/ASRM also cites an NIH trial (174 men) that did not show enough effect on semen parameters or DNA integrity to proceed to full accrual.

items.stem: How do the positions of ESHRE (unexplained infertility) and NICE on antioxidants for men compare?

options.text: Both recommend them for elevated fragmentation.
options.why: NICE explicitly advises against offering them to improve DNA integrity.

options.text: ESHRE advises against them with a strong recommendation based on many RCTs in men.
options.why: It is conditional, and the review it relies on included only 2 RCTs and 133 women: there are very few direct data in men.

options.text: ESHRE: probably not recommended as adjuncts during fertility treatment (conditional); NICE: do not offer supplements, antioxidants or medical treatments to improve sperm DNA integrity.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE 2023 (conditional) and NICE 1.24.6, which is more specific.

options.text: NICE recommends them and ESHRE does not address them.
options.why: NICE advises against offering them and ESHRE does address them (conditional against).

items.explanation: Same direction, different wording and scope: read each recommendation with its population and strength.

items.stem: A man with a normal semen analysis in a couple with idiopathic infertility cites the 2022 Cochrane review to justify taking antioxidants. Which limitation is key?

options.text: The review included only men with azoospermia.
options.why: It included subfertile men (90 RCTs; 10,303 men), not only men with azoospermia.

options.text: The review showed that antioxidants are harmful.
options.why: It showed no harm for miscarriage; only mild gastrointestinal discomfort.

options.text: The review excluded men with idiopathic infertility and normal semen parameters: it does not apply to him.
options.why: Correct: it is an exclusion criterion of the review (men with idiopathic infertility and normal semen parameters), in addition to the limitations the authors state: risk of bias, imprecision and few studies reporting live birth.

options.text: None: the review applies to any man.
options.why: The authors explicitly excluded men with idiopathic infertility and normal semen parameters.

items.explanation: Before applying a review, check its population: this one does not include men with a normal semen analysis.

items.stem: In the 2022 Cochrane review of antioxidants in subfertile men, which adverse effect is described?

options.text: Mild gastrointestinal discomfort (OR 2.70; 95% CI 1.46–4.99; low certainty).
options.why: Correct: 16 RCTs; low certainty.

options.text: More miscarriages (OR 1.46; 95% CI 0.75–2.83).
options.why: That interval includes 1: there was no difference in miscarriage.

options.text: Severe hepatotoxicity.
options.why: The review does not describe that effect.

options.text: None: the review did not assess adverse effects.
options.why: It did assess adverse effects and described mild gastrointestinal discomfort.

items.explanation: Honest message: probably not harmful (AUA/ASRM), but with possible mild digestive discomfort (Cochrane, low certainty).

items.stem: The Cochrane review estimates that, with a 16% baseline live birth, antioxidants would bring it to between 17% and 27%. Which caveat matters?

options.text: It comes from large RCTs with high certainty.
options.why: These are 12 small or medium-sized studies with very low certainty.

options.text: It refers to clinical pregnancy, not live birth.
options.why: The estimate is for live birth; clinical pregnancy has its own OR (1.89).

options.text: It stays the same after excluding high risk-of-bias studies.
options.why: When they are excluded, the Peto OR is 1.22 (95% CI 0.85–1.75), not significant.

options.text: It is based on only 246 live births from 12 small or medium-sized studies, with very low certainty.
options.why: Correct: moreover, the effect is no longer significant when high risk-of-bias studies are excluded.

items.explanation: Faced with an attractive absolute figure, ask how many events it comes from, with what certainty, and whether it survives excluding bias.

items.stem: He asks whether he must give up alcohol completely to improve his semen. What does NICE advise?

options.text: Any amount of alcohol reduces male fertility.
options.why: NICE states that drinking within low-risk limits is unlikely to affect semen quality.

options.text: Excessive alcohol intake is detrimental to semen quality; drinking within the UK low-risk limits (14 units per week, spread across several days) is unlikely to affect it.
options.why: Correct: this is NICE's advice on alcohol for men.

options.text: Alcohol has no relation to semen quality.
options.why: NICE states that excessive intake is detrimental to semen quality.

options.text: He can drink up to 28 units per week without effect.
options.why: The low-risk limit NICE cites is 14 units per week.

items.explanation: A proportionate message: avoid excess, without promising that total abstinence will improve fertility.

items.stem: Which of these statements about male lifestyle factors matches what NICE advises?

options.text: Elevated scrotal temperature is associated with reduced semen quality, but it is uncertain whether loose-fitting underwear improves fertility.
options.why: Correct: this is how NICE puts it.

options.text: Caffeine causes fertility problems and should be stopped.
options.why: NICE states that there is no consistent evidence of an association between caffeine and fertility problems.

options.text: Smoking has been shown to cause male infertility.
options.why: NICE says smoking is associated with reduced semen quality, although its impact on fertility is uncertain; stopping improves general health.

options.text: Weight does not affect male fertility.
options.why: NICE states that a BMI ≥30 kg/m² carries an increased risk of reduced fertility.

items.explanation: Each habit has its own nuance in NICE: separate “associated with poorer semen” from “shown to improve fertility when changed”.

items.title: Case: Carla, Diego and the semen analysis that does not add up

steps.text: Carla (fictional case), 33, regular cycles; Diego, 36. They have been trying for 15 months. You assess both concurrently. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] Diego’s first semen analysis (complete sample, 4 days of abstinence, quality-controlled laboratory) shows a concentration of 10 × 10⁶/ml and a total number of 20 × 10⁶ per ejaculate, both below the WHO 5th centile (16 × 10⁶/ml and 39 × 10⁶ respectively). [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]]

Repeat and clinical work-up: the semen analysis repeated at 3 months confirms 8 × 10⁶/ml, without azoospermia. Diego denies drugs or gym products, which NICE asks to enquire about. With 2 or more abnormal semen analyses, NICE offers examination of the scrotum and testes and suggests considering testosterone and gonadotrophins. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Findings: there is a palpable left varicocele; morning testosterone and gonadotrophins are within the laboratory range. At 8 × 10⁶/ml the karyotype and Y-microdeletion thresholds of neither guideline are met. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] Diego and Carla ask whether sperm DNA fragmentation “will decide whether ICSI is needed”. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]]

Varicocele: they fit the profile in which AUA/ASRM and NICE contemplate repair (palpable, abnormal parameters, spontaneous conception). You present the benefit as an estimate with uncertainty: pregnancy data come largely from non-randomised studies and live-birth data are scarce. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

A friend suggests testosterone “to wake up the testes”. You explain that AUA/ASRM advises against prescribing it to someone seeking fertility because it can suppress spermatogenesis, and that NICE advises against offering androgens for semen abnormalities. To reinforce the idea, think about what you would tell another man who already uses it and has azoospermia. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Antioxidants: Diego brings the Cochrane headline (live-birth OR 1.43). Together you review the very low certainty and the analysis without high risk-of-bias studies (Peto OR 1.22; 95% CI 0.85–1.75). [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

Decision: Diego wants to take a supplement. It is explained that AUA/ASRM considers its usefulness questionable and probably not harmful, and that Cochrane recorded mild digestive discomfort. It is agreed that it will not delay the rest of the couple’s work-up. [[ref:aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility]] [[ref:deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants]]

Closing: you explain that no isolated value “decides” fertility, that the plan rests on the whole picture (history, examination, hormones, varicocele and Carla’s work-up), and that supplement results should be judged by pregnancy and live birth, not only by semen parameters. [[ref:who-2021-semen-manual]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.title: Optimizing natural fertility: a committee opinion
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine; Practice Committee of the Society for Reproductive Endocrinology and Infertility
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.population: Couples or individuals attempting conception with no evidence of infertility; Fertil Steril 2022;117:53–63.
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.finding: Monthly fecundability greatest in the first 3 months; relative fertility at 40 about half that of the late 20s/early 30s; semen parameters decline after 35, but male fertility does not appear appreciably affected before ~50. Fertile window: 6 days ending on the day of ovulation; intercourse every 1–2 days gives the highest rates and 2–3 times per week nearly equivalent; do not limit frequency. Position and postcoital routines have no impact; insufficient evidence that a specific diet improves natural fertility.
asrm-2022-optimizing-natural-fertility.limitations: Full text read (ASRM PDF). Committee opinion based on expert consensus; most lifestyle data are observational; US context.

aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.title: Diagnosis and Treatment of Infertility in Men: AUA/ASRM Guideline (2020; amended 2024)
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.authors: American Urological Association; American Society for Reproductive Medicine (Schlegel PN, Sigman M, Collura B, et al.)
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.population: Male partners of couples with infertility.
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.finding: Statement 1: concurrent assessment of both partners in the initial evaluation (Expert Opinion). Statement 2: reproductive history (Clinical Principle) and one or more semen analyses in the initial male evaluation (Strong Recommendation; Evidence Level Grade B). Statement 7: advise couples with advanced paternal age (≥40) of an increased risk of adverse health outcomes for offspring (Expert Opinion).
aua-asrm-2020-male-infertility.limitations: Official AUA page read: summary of all guideline statements and discussion on semen analysis, hormones, DNA fragmentation, pregnancy loss, imaging, varicocele, testosterone and supplements. Statement numbers do not always appear in the extracted text; Part I/II DOIs not verified. US context.

deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.title: Antioxidants for male subfertility
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.authors: de Ligny W, Smits RM, Mackenzie-Proctor R, Jordan V, Fleischer K, de Bruin JP, Showell MG
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.population: 90 RCTs, 10,303 subfertile men (aged 18–65) of couples attending fertility clinics, some undergoing assisted reproduction; 20 different oral antioxidants. Excluded men with idiopathic infertility and normal semen parameters. Search to 15 Feb 2021. Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2022;5:CD007411.
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.finding: Live birth: OR 1.43 (95% CI 1.07–1.91; 12 RCTs; 1283 men; very low certainty; 246 live births); with a 16% baseline, 17–27% with antioxidants. Excluding high risk-of-bias studies: no evidence of increase (Peto OR 1.22; 95% CI 0.85–1.75; 8 RCTs; 827 men). Clinical pregnancy: OR 1.89 (1.45–2.47; 20 RCTs; 1706 men; low certainty). Miscarriage: no difference (OR 1.46; 0.75–2.83; 6 RCTs; very low certainty). Mild gastrointestinal discomfort: OR 2.70 (1.46–4.99; 16 RCTs; low certainty). Only 20 of 67 meta-analysed studies reported clinical pregnancy and 12 live birth. Authors' conclusion: overall evidence inconclusive owing to serious risk of bias and imprecision.
deligny-2022-cochrane-male-antioxidants.limitations: Full abstract read (Europe PMC, PMID 35506389; text saved in the source library), including the sensitivity analysis and the authors’ conclusions; ESHRE add-ons 2023 reproduces the live-birth, miscarriage and gastrointestinal figures. Full text, GRADE tables and semen-parameter results not read. Antioxidants and doses highly heterogeneous; excluded men with idiopathic infertility and normal semen parameters.

eshre-2022-rpl.title: ESHRE guideline: recurrent pregnancy loss: an update in 2022
eshre-2022-rpl.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on RPL; Bender Atik R, Christiansen OB, Elson J, et al.
eshre-2022-rpl.population: Couples with recurrent pregnancy loss (two or more losses).
eshre-2022-rpl.finding: Low-dose folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss in unexplained RPL (strong); do not use high doses without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions raising NTD risk (diabetes, epilepsy). Prophylactic vitamin D may be considered in preconception counselling (GPP) although evidence of effectiveness is absent; vitamin D testing to find a cause is not recommended. Multivitamins: advise options safe in pregnancy (GPP); they are not a treatment. Sperm DNA fragmentation in couples with RPL: could be considered for diagnostic purposes, using a validated test (conditional; ⊕⊕⊕○). Parental karyotyping: not routine; can be carried out after an individual risk assessment (conditional).
eshre-2022-rpl.limitations: Recommendations table and vitamin D chapter read in the full ESHRE PDF. Specific RPL population; several recommendations are good practice points (GPP), not trial-based. Recommendations on sperm DNA fragmentation and parental karyotyping checked in the HRO summary (hoad002) and in the justification of the full PDF. The guideline is the 2022 update (final version January 2023; HRO summary 2023); the module cites it as ESHRE 2022.

eshre-2023-addons.title: Good practice recommendations on add-ons in reproductive medicine
eshre-2023-addons.authors: ESHRE Add-ons Working Group; Lundin K, Bentzen JG, Bozdag G, Ebner T, Harper J, Le Clef N, Moffett A, Norcross S, Polyzos NP, Rautakallio-Hokkanen S, Sfontouris I, Sermon K, Vermeulen N, Pinborg A
eshre-2023-addons.population: Patients undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART); Hum Reprod 2023 (ESHRE Pages).
eshre-2023-addons.finding: 42 recommendations using its own four-phrase scale (recommended; can be considered; currently not recommended for routine clinical use; not recommended). Peripheral blood immune tests and uterine NK-cell testing: not recommended. Screening hysteroscopy: currently not recommended for routine clinical use (can be considered in recurrent implantation failure). Sperm DNA damage testing, endometrial scratching and KIR/HLA genotyping: currently not recommended for routine clinical use. ICSI for non-male factor infertility: not recommended.
eshre-2023-addons.limitations: Full text read (UCL Discovery open-access copy of the advance online version); the wording of every cited recommendation and the scale-definition table were checked verbatim. Good practice recommendations based on review and consensus, not a GRADE guideline: no recommendation rests on high-quality evidence and only four on moderate-quality evidence. ART population, not specifically unexplained infertility.

eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.title: Evidence-based guideline: unexplained infertility
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.authors: ESHRE Guideline Group on Unexplained Infertility; Romualdi D, et al.
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.finding: With regular cycles, ovarian reserve testing is not required to identify the aetiology of infertility or to predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong recommendation, low certainty). IUI with ovarian stimulation first line (strong, very low certainty). ICSI not recommended over conventional IVF (rec. 42, strong, ⊕); endometrial scratching should not be offered (rec. 45, strong, ⊕⊕); adjunct oral antioxidants in women probably not recommended (rec. 46, conditional, ⊕).
eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility.limitations: Search up to October 2022; many recommendations with low or very low certainty. Full text read (journal summary via Europe PMC PMC10546081 and the full 114-page ESHRE guideline).

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse. Unexplained fertility problems: keep trying for 2 years in total before treatment (1.38.1); do not offer ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment (1.38.2); then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.38.3). Male factor: repeat an abnormal semen analysis, ideally at 3 months (1.17.4); do not test sperm DNA fragmentation (1.17.6); do not offer androgens (1.24.3). Endometriosis: expectant management for up to 2 years (including time already spent trying) or surgery; then consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offer IVF (1.36.1–1.36.3). Add-ons: do not offer endometrial scratch or hysteroscopy as pre-treatment (1.40.1–1.40.2), endometrial receptivity testing (1.41.1), immunological agents (1.42.1) or PGT-A (1.48.1); do not offer assisted hatching (1.49.1, from 2004); ICSI: offer with surgically retrieved sperm or frozen–thawed oocytes, consider with abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation, and do not use without male factor (1.50.1–1.50.5).
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.

who-2021-semen-manual.title: WHO laboratory manual for the examination and processing of human semen, sixth edition
who-2021-semen-manual.population: Laboratory manual. Reference population (Campbell et al.): about 3500 men from 12 countries whose partners achieved a natural conception with time to pregnancy ≤12 months and 2–7 days of abstinence; excludes men attending infertility clinics. ISBN 978-92-4-003078-7.
who-2021-semen-manual.finding: Table 8.3 (5th centile; 95% CI): volume 1.4 ml (1.3–1.5); concentration 16 × 10⁶/ml (15–18); total number 39 × 10⁶/ejaculate (35–40); total motility 42% (40–43); progressive 30% (29–31); vitality 54% (50–56); normal forms 4% (3.9–4.0). The lower fifth centile does not represent a limit between fertile and infertile men (8.1.3); there is substantial overlap between them; the manual is not a guideline for clinical decisions and clinically useful decision limits are still lacking (8.1, 8.1.2.2). The 2–7-day abstinence recommendation is based on clinical experience and may contribute to variability (ch. 2). Distinguishing 3% from 5% normal forms in an individual requires assessing 1500 spermatozoa (ch. 2).
who-2021-semen-manual.limitations: Read in the text of the official WHO PDF (292 pages, copy in the source library): introduction 1.3; chapter 2 (factors influencing the ejaculate, 2–7-day abstinence, collection, counting and morphology); 3.2.1 (DNA fragmentation, as a technique and background only); and all of 8.1 with Tables 8.1–8.3 (pp. 211–213). Technical laboratory manual, not a clinical guideline; reference population of men whose partners conceived within ≤12 months, not of infertile couples; the manual calls these figures the “lower fifth percentile” (ESHRE and AUA/ASRM call them the fifth-percentile reference limit or lower reference limit). The remaining laboratory procedures were not read.
